metadata.title: Lines and Shine
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: How to draw a line at any angle and make it shine
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.
metadata.source_doc: Godot 4.7 documentation; Godot 4.7.2 runs on Apple M4 Pro (evidence/planning-checks); see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Lines and Shine. Learn how a shader draws a line at any angle from one rule, and how to slide that line across a sprite as a shine.

routing.reason: The lecture skill's approved first beat: portrait, title, narrated summary.

shot.visual_intent: Professor Bear portrait, exact film title and short payoff visible immediately.

show.event: Complete populated lecture opener visible for the whole narration

qc.sparse_reason: Identity card: portrait and title; teaching motion resumes in BIDEA.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Most people think a line needs two points, one at each end. A shader has no pen. It gets one rule, and every pixel asks it: am I on the line?
beats.motion_claim: The writer types the assumption a newcomer arrives with and corrects it into the film's real subject.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. A pixel is one dot of the picture. U V is a pixel's address on the shape: zero to one across, zero to one down. A uniform is a value your game sets, the same for every pixel. Slope is how steeply a line rises. Alpha is how visible a pixel is.

terms.meaning: one dot of the picture on screen
a point's address on the shape: 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down
a value your game sets from outside; every pixel sees the same one
how steeply a line rises: up divided by across
how visible a pixel is: 0 invisible, 1 solid

beats.act: I · A Line as a Test
beats.narration_text: This glint is where we are heading. No stripe is drawn anywhere. Every pixel measures how far it sits from a line, and the pixels that are close light up. By the end, you will write that rule yourself.

beats.act: I · A Line as a Test
beats.narration_text: From school: a line is y equals m x plus b. The m is the slope, the climb for each step across. The b is its starting height. Make the line pass through the middle, and b is zero.

shot.visual_intent: Axes on the cream stage with a warm-grey line y = m x + b crossing the vertical axis above the origin, a terracotta dot marking b. A right triangle (one step across, m up) rides along the line under the label 'slope m: up per step across'. Then the line slides down until it passes through the origin: the b dot lands on 0 and the label becomes 'y = m x'.

line slides to the middle; b = 0

shot.motion_claim: The slope triangle rides along the line, then b shrinks to zero as the line settles through the middle.

beats.act: I · A Line as a Test
beats.narration_text: A pixel's address, U V, has its zero at the top left corner. Double it, subtract one, and the zero lands in the middle. The address now runs from minus one to one, both ways.

A terracotta dot sits at the top-left corner. The labels morph to -1, 0 and 1 and the dot glides to the middle; the formula 'p = UV × 2 − 1' appears under the square.

beats.act: I · A Line as a Test
beats.narration_text: One more change. Godot counts the address downward, so flip the second number. Now up is up, and a positive slope climbs to the right, the way you learned it.

beats.act: I · A Line as a Test
beats.narration_text: Now turn the line into a question. Move everything to one side: y minus m times x. On the line, the answer is exactly zero. Anywhere else, it is not, and any pixel can check.

shot.visual_intent: Left: the equation 'y = m x'. The 'm x' term travels across the equals sign and the equation becomes 'y − m x = 0', captioned 'the test'. Right: the square with the line m = 0.5 and a terracotta dot riding along it, labelled '0'; then a second dot off the line reads +0.6.

beats.act: I · A Line as a Test
beats.narration_text: Try a slope of one half. A point on the line gives zero. Straight above it, plus point six. Straight below, minus point six. The sign tells you the side. The size is the gap, straight up or down.

beats.act: I · A Line as a Test
beats.narration_text: Slide a point along a parallel line, and the answer never changes. Plus point six stays plus point six. So the test gives one number to a whole line of pixels, parallel to ours.

beats.act: I · A Line as a Test
beats.narration_text: As a shader, fragment runs once for every pixel of the card. Red rises where the answer is positive, so that side looks warm. Blue rises where it is negative, so it looks cool. Pixels on the line stay grey.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left (the ten-line shader) whose first two lines carry one-line labels ('shader_type canvas_item: the first line says this shader is for 2D drawing', 'fragment(): runs once for each pixel the shape covers; sets its color'); at right a real Godot window with a square card showing the signed test: warm at the upper left, cool at the lower right, a grey strip between. Three readouts land on the card at the three points from the drawing: +0.6, 0 and −0.6.

beats.narration_text: We think in angles, not slopes, and the tangent connects them. Go one step across, along a line turned by the angle. The height you climb is the tangent, and that height is the slope.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Slope from an Angle' (serif 40) top-left. Axes, a warm-grey line through the origin and a pale grey filled wedge for its angle. At across = 1 a warm-grey dashed vertical runs from the axis up to the line, ending in a terracotta dot; its height is a live number. The angle grows from 0 to 60 degrees and the height reads 0, 0.58, 1.0 and 1.73. Labels: 'angle', 'one step across', 'tangent of the angle = the slope'.

beats.narration_text: In the shader, the slope is the tangent of the angle. Godot's tangent works in radians, where a full turn is about six point two eight, so the radians function converts our degrees first.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left with the slope line highlighted; at right a real Godot card whose grey strip turns, climbing to the right, as the angle sweeps from 0 to 60 degrees. Readouts: '0°: m = 0' at the start and '45°: m = 1' as it passes 45.

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · angle swept by script
props.caption: radians: a full turn is about 6.28

shot.motion_claim: The strip turns and the readouts give the slope at 0 and 45 degrees.

lecture.why: The line turning with the angle uniform is the claim the code makes; the readouts tie the picture to the number.
lecture.capture_spec: C04: Lab card, 02-angle-line, angle 0 to 60 linearly over the clip (6 s); angle is 45 at 75 percent. GPU slopes: 0.57735 (30), 1.0 (45), 1.73205 (60).

beats.narration_text: What if we skip that conversion? Godot reads thirty degrees as thirty radians. The slope becomes minus six point four: a steep line, leaning the wrong way. If an angle looks wrong, check the radians first.

shot.visual_intent: Two real Godot cards side by side on the stage, the same angle sweeping to 30 degrees. Left: the grey strip climbs gently to the right (m = 0.58). Right: the strip is steep and leans the other way (m = -6.4). Below, the two code lines that differ; a terracotta ring settles on the right card.

props.code:
float m = tan(radians(angle));
float m = tan(angle);

beats.narration_text: A line has no thickness, so we cannot see it. Keep every pixel whose answer is near zero, and you get a band around the line. Two tools do that: absolute value drops the sign, and step is a switch.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Distance to the Line' (serif 40) top-left. Left: the test square with the warm-grey line m = 0.5; a pale grey band grows out around the line (the pixels whose answer is near zero), labelled 'a band'. Right, arriving after the band: two small plots. abs(x) as a V with a terracotta dot sliding along x and its height mirrored, labelled 'abs: drop the sign'; step(a, b) as a flat zero that jumps to one where b reaches a, a dot sliding along b, labelled 'step(a, b): 0 until b reaches a, then 1' and the docs rule 'b < a ? 0.0 : 1.0'.

beats.narration_text: Take the absolute value of the test and call it d, for distance. Then step: distance first, thickness second. It answers one when the thickness has reached the distance, so the pixel is inside the band. Otherwise, zero.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left; at right a real Godot card with a white diagonal band across a grey card, climbing to the right. Two readouts on the card: '1' on the band and '0' beside it.

beats.narration_text: Why? The test measures straight up from the line. Distance means the shortest way, at a right angle. Tilt the line, and the shortest way gets shorter than straight up. The steeper the line, the bigger the difference.

shot.visual_intent: A warm-grey line through the origin and a terracotta dot above it. A light-grey dashed vertical from the dot to the line (label 'straight up 0.6') and a darker solid grey segment at a right angle (label 'shortest way'). The line tilts from 0 to 60 degrees while the point rides with it so the vertical gap stays 0.6; the right-angle segment shrinks and its label reads 0.60, 0.42, 0.30.

beats.narration_text: The fix is one right triangle. Along the line, one step across climbs m, so that step is the square root of one plus m squared long. Divide the test by that, and you have the shortest distance.

shot.visual_intent: A right triangle with legs 1 (across) and 0.5 (up) along a warm-grey line, the long side labelled 'sqrt(1 + 0.5²) = 1.118' (sqrt: the square root). Beside it a second, same-shaped triangle at the point: the straight-up gap 0.6 as its long side. An arrow labelled '÷ 1.118' turns 0.6 into 0.54, 'the shortest distance'.

lecture.why: The divide is a similar-triangles fact; two triangles of one shape make it visible, a formula alone would not.

beats.narration_text: In code: absolute value of the test, divided by the square root of one plus m times m. Thickness is now a real distance. Point one makes the band a tenth of the card wide.

beats.narration_text: To slide the line, add an offset to the distance, before the absolute value. The distance is true, so the line moves exactly that far, straight across, at any angle. Offset point five is a quarter of the card.

Final hold: readouts 'offset 0.5' and '¼ of card'.

beats.narration_text: You may see another way: subtract a center point before testing. How far that slides the line depends on the angle. Shift a flat line sideways, and nothing moves. The offset slides it straight across, whatever the angle.

shot.visual_intent: Two real Godot cards side by side, a flat white band across each. Left: the center shifted across from -0.6 to 0.6; the band does not move. Right: the offset swept the same way; the band slides up and down. Readouts under the cards: 'center: no move' and 'offset: slides'.

beats.narration_text: Now the sprite. Where the band is, blend the sprite's color toward white. Mix takes two colors and a weight: zero gives the first, one gives the second. Here, the weight is the band.

beats.narration_text: To start a shine when something happens, let your game drive the offset. Set the start, then tween to the end; a tween glides a value over time. Skip that first line, and the tween has nothing to start from.

props.code:
func shine():
	var mat: ShaderMaterial = $Sprite.material
	mat.set_shader_parameter("offset", -1.5)
	create_tween().tween_property(mat, "shader_parameter/offset", 1.5, 0.8)

beats.narration_text: It is the same distance in disguise. In our triangle, the cosine is one over that square root, so dividing by it is multiplying by the cosine. What is left is exactly p dot n.

shot.visual_intent: An equation chain, one line at a time, each line rewriting the one above: '(y − m x) ÷ sqrt(1 + m²)' → '(y − m x) × cosine' → 'y × cosine − x × sine' → 'p · n'. Beside it the earlier triangle (1, m, sqrt(1 + m²)) with cosine = 1 ÷ sqrt(1 + m²) marked on it.

beats.narration_text: In code, the normal is minus sine, cosine of the angle, and the distance is the absolute value of p dot n. No tangent, no divide. At thirty, sixty and eighty-nine degrees, it matches the slope version pixel for pixel.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A line is a test: y minus m times x is zero on it, positive on one side, negative on the other. The slope is the tangent of the angle, and it blows up at vertical. Divide the test by the square root of one plus m squared and it becomes the true distance. A step makes the band, an offset slides it, and alpha keeps the shine on the sprite. A direction and a dot give the same distance, with no seam at vertical. A line is one rule, and a shine is that rule, slid.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Write a Godot canvas item shader for a sprite. Uniforms: angle in degrees, thickness, offset. Center the address and flip it so up is up. Draw a white band along a line through the middle at that angle, slid sideways by the offset, the same thickness at every angle, only on visible pixels. Finally, point me to the distance line. Then check two things yourself. At forty-five degrees, does the band climb to the right? And is it as thick at eighty degrees as at ten?
